The season header and the approach variant's season were the only fields excluding July.

Every source (club scramble reports, trip reports, Wikipedia) climbs Carrie from Sol Duc via the High Divide, the Catwalk and the southwest ridge / south-facing basin; none describes a Hurricane Ridge approach. The overview already states the name is misleading. The route name is out of scope for patching, and aspect 'SE' is tied to that name; the true climbing aspect (SW ridge, S-facing basin) needs an owner decision on renaming, so no patch.

earlier_research.evidence: USGS 3DEP ground elevation at the mapped Boston Charlie's Camp point is ~5,543 ft (matching bivy[3].elev), which leaves only ~1,450 ft to the 6,995 ft summit; but the widely repeated route description says the southwest ridge gains 2,000 ft in under a mile from the camp, and the same figure is also in pitch_detail[3].notes (not only the bivy card). No second source gives either the camp's elevation or a different gain figure, so neither copy is changed; a topo-derived camp elevation from a second source, or a trip report stating the camp-to-summit gain, would settle it.

row.overview: Mount Carrie is the highest point of the Bailey Range and the scenic centerpiece of the classic Bailey Range Traverse. There is no trail or known route connecting Hurricane Ridge to Cat Basin or Mount Carrie — Hurricane Ridge sits on the opposite (east) side of the park and is used only as a distant viewpoint of Carrie's glaciated north face. Every recorded ascent instead approaches from the Sol Duc River Road trailhead on the park's north side, via Heart Lake, High Divide, Cat Basin, the exposed "Catwalk" ridge crossing, and Boston Charlie's Camp, before gaining Carrie's southwest ridge and a broad south-facing scree basin to the summit.
row.beta: This route gains the High Divide crest from Heart Lake, then heads east along the Cat Basin trail toward Cat Peak before crossing the Catwalk—an infamous, exposed ridge-top connecting Cat Peak to Mount Carrie. The Catwalk features high Class 2 to low Class 3 scrambling with substantial exposure; a fall here can be fatal. Beyond the Catwalk, the route follows the southwest ridge of Mount Carrie, initially grassy but becoming a mixture of grass and rock outcroppings at higher elevations, traversing scree and possible snow to the true summit at the far right of the summit basin.
row.turnaround: On snow, top out before midday softening; the long return to camp makes an early turnaround wise.
row.face: Long Ridge / Bailey Range crest approach
row.permit: Olympic National Park: no permit for day climbs; all overnight wilderness stays require a wilderness camping permit via Recreation.gov.
row.comms: Cell phone coverage is unreliable throughout Olympic National Park. Satellite communicator (Garmin InReach or similar) is strongly recommended.
row.descent: Reverse the southwest ridge and south-facing scree basin down to Boston Charlie's Camp, re-cross the exposed Catwalk to Cat Peak, then follow High Divide back to Heart Lake and out the Sol Duc River Trail to the trailhead.
obj_haz: exposed unroped scrambling on the Catwalk

The maintained trail toward Sol Duc Falls and the Deer Lake junction leaves from here.

row.detailed_rack: A lightweight alpine rack for scrambling: ice axe, crampons, helmet, rope (30–50m rope optional for group safety on Catwalk), and self-rescue equipment. Harness and sling recommended if roping. For water-crossing sections, consider trekking poles for stream fords.
what_to_bring: Layers (high-altitude, wet Pacific weather is common)
High-calorie food and electrolyte drink mix
First aid kit with blister treatment
pro_tips: Start early from Boston Charlie's Camp to ensure you cross the Catwalk in daylight and have time to retreat if weather deteriorates.
Scout the Catwalk carefully in marginal light; the exposure is real and requires full attention.
The loose rock (choss) is typical of the Olympics—expect to pick your way carefully and wear a helmet.
Descending is often more hazardous than ascending on scrambles; move methodically on the way down.
Cache water bottles at Boston Charlie's to avoid carrying excessive weight; melt snow or find streams at higher elevations.
Wildlife is active at dawn and dusk; make noise while traveling.
watch_out: The Catwalk is the crux of the climb—treat it with respect and expect high exposure.
Helmet is mandatory; rockfall is frequent from loose, unstable rock.
Before mid-July, expect deep snow on the Catwalk; ice axe and crampons required.
Wildlife encounter risk; black bears present in the area.
Cell phone coverage is unreliable; carry satellite communication device for emergencies.
row.pro_needs: Grade Class 2–3 scrambling protection: helmet mandatory for rockfall hazard, ice axe essential for early-season snow and self-arrest, crampons for frozen surfaces June–July. Rope carries psychological security on the Catwalk but is not strictly required for individuals with solid scrambling skills and comfort with exposure; recommended for groups.
row.best_season: Late July through mid-September for the most reliable dry scree and a snow-free Catwalk crossing; an ice axe is still worth carrying for lingering snow patches into July.
row.approach: There is no established route to Mount Carrie from Hurricane Ridge; that area is separated from the Bailey Range by miles of trailless, glaciated terrain and functions only as a viewpoint. The actual approach used by essentially all climbers starts at the Sol Duc River Road trailhead (~2,000 ft) on US-101 near Lake Crescent: Sol Duc Falls → Deer Lake Trail junction (+1 mi) → Heart Lake (+7 mi, 4,800 ft) → High Divide crest (+0.5 mi, 5,100 ft) → east on the Cat Basin trail toward Cat Basin → an unmaintained path over Cat Peak's exposed south side and across the airy "Catwalk" ridge (Class 3) to Boston Charlie's Camp. From camp, the final push follows Carrie's southwest ridge (Class 1 grass/rock) and contours a broad, steep, loose south-facing scree basin around 6,500 ft before a scree-and-snow finish (ice axe advisable) to the summit (Class 2). One-way distance from the trailhead to the summit is roughly 13 miles.
row.descent_text: Reverse the ascent line. From the summit, descend the southwest ridge and the south-facing scree basin below it to Boston Charlie's Camp, keeping the helmet on - the rock here is loose and rockfall is the reason the helmet is mandatory on this route - and carrying the axe for any steep snow still lying in the basin early in the season. From Boston Charlie's, re-cross the Catwalk to Cat Peak. This is the crux of the day in descent exactly as it is in ascent: a narrow rock and heather ridge with substantial exposure where a fall could be fatal, and descending a scramble is generally the more hazardous direction, so cross it in daylight and with full attention rather than hurrying it at the end of a long day. From Cat Peak follow the High Divide back to Heart Lake, then take the Sol Duc River Trail out to the trailhead. There is no rappelling anywhere on the standard line.
row.bail: Retreat into Cat Basin is feasible; the main commitment is the distance back to the road.

pitch_detail.notes: From the Sol Duc road-end trailhead (~2,000 ft) pass Sol Duc Falls and the Deer Lake junction (about 1 mile) and climb about 7 more miles up the Sol Duc valley to Heart Lake (4,800 ft). The lake has several good camps; a wilderness permit and bear canister are required, and permits here are in heavy demand.
pitch_detail.pitch: Sol Duc TH to Heart Lake

pitch_detail.notes: Climb about half a mile to the High Divide crest (~5,100 ft) and follow it toward Cat Basin, about 3 miles, to where the maintained trail ends. A thin, worn path continues along the ridge below Cat Peak through trees and brush to the start of the Catwalk. Late in the season water up here is limited to snowbanks and sinkholes, so carry enough.

A narrow rock and heather ridgetop links Cat Peak to the Bailey Range: high class 2 to low class 3 moves with serious exposure, where a fall could be fatal. Before mid-July lingering snow can make it much harder. Past it, push through brush to Boston Charlie's Camp, a small, sloping, exposed site with a brackish sinkhole pond; filter the water, and treat it as an emergency bivy rather than a planned camp.

A semi-cairned path switchbacks up Carrie's southwest ridge, about 2,000 ft in under a mile; grassy at first, then grass and rock outcrops as it narrows. Near 6,500 ft it contours around the top of a big south-facing scree basin ringed with summits; the rock is loose, so helmets on. The true summit is at the far right (east) side of the basin, reached via the summit ridge. Early season, snow in the basin calls for an axe.

itinerary.cal: Best mid-July through mid-September once snow clears enough for safe passage across the exposed Catwalk; earlier in the season an ice axe is needed in the summit scree basin.

weather.probability: Weather can shift quickly in this interior range; summer is the best window with the snow finger receding through the season

approach_variants.name: Sol Duc road end, High Divide and Cat Basin to the Catwalk
approach_variants.notes: Start at the road-end trailhead on the hot-springs road on the park's north side. Hike past the falls, on past the Deer Lake junction, and up to Heart Lake — the last reliable water. Climb to the High Divide crest and follow the primitive trail east from the junction above the lake toward Cat Basin, then take the unmaintained path over the exposed south side of the peak beyond it and across the CATWALK to the first camp on its far side. Do NOT plan an approach from Hurricane Ridge: it is a viewpoint separated from this range by miles of trailless glaciated terrain and there is no established route to this peak from it.
approach_variants.season: Late July to September, once the high traverse is clear of snow; an ice axe is still worth carrying for the summit basin.
hazards: The Catwalk — exposed, sharp, and a fall there could be fatal
Thin, crumbly ledges with major exposure on the south side of the peak just before the Catwalk
Steep, loose, unstable scree in the summit basin
Early-season snow in the basin, where an ice axe is advisable
No water between Heart Lake and the summit
Unmaintained and unsigned beyond the divide, requiring solid off-trail route-finding
approach_variants.baseFinding: From the basin camp, the line follows the peak's SOUTHWEST RIDGE — grassy and rocky walking at first — and the base of the real climbing is where that ridge stops being walkable crest and you have to CONTOUR OFF IT into a broad, steep, loose SOUTH-FACING SCREE BASIN at around sixty-five hundred feet. The test that you are in the right basin: it is loose, unstable scree in the sun, and the TRUE SUMMIT sits at its FAR RIGHT-HAND END, not at the high point directly above where you enter it. Finish on scree and snow. Negative markers: if you have roped up and are travelling on ice with crevasses, you are on the glacier variation on the northeast side of the peak; if you are still walking a grassy crest with no need to leave it, you have not reached the contour yet and are short of the basin.

bivy.name: Heart Lake
bivy.notes: The most useful camp in the whole zone for a climber. It sits just under eight miles in, a short climb below the High Divide, and it is the last camp on maintained trail with easy water before the route to Mount Carrie, Ruth Peak and Mount Fairchild leaves the trail for good. From here you gain the divide, follow it past Cat Peak, cross the exposed class 3 ridge known as the Catwalk, and the climbing starts. Parties who miss the permit sometimes take a Seven Lakes Basin camp such as Lunch Lake instead, but that puts you off the direct line and adds side-hilling in the morning. Fill every bottle here — the stretch from the divide out to the first Bailey Range camps carries no running water.
bivy.water: Reliable — the lake and the creek feeding it, all season; this is the last dependable running water for a long way
bivy.permit: Olympic wilderness permit required, QUOTA camp booked for a specific night on the federal booking site. Reservations for the summer season open in the spring and the High Divide camps are among the fastest to go in the park, often within minutes. Bear canisters mandatory, no campfires.
bivy.capacity: A small number of designated sites under a nightly cap, with a vault toilet; group parties must use the designated group site

bivy.name: Cat Basin
bivy.notes: Cat Basin lies just below the junction at roughly 5,042 ft where the High Divide trail meets the way into the Bailey Range, so it is the last sheltered ground on the approach before the route turns cross-country beneath Cat Peak. Parties heading for Mount Carrie use it to shorten the following morning and to get below the wind, since the divide itself is fully exposed. It is genuinely primitive — expect to be finding your own flat spot on durable ground, and expect the sites to be scattered rather than obvious. In heavy snow years the basin fills late and the traverse out to the Catwalk holds steep snow well into July.
bivy.water: Streams in the basin early in the season, unreliable by late summer; carry from Heart Lake if the year has been dry
bivy.permit: Olympic wilderness permit required. This one is worth phoning the park's wilderness information office about rather than assuming — the primitive and cross-country parts of this area are not all bookable through the standard online map, and staff issue those permits directly. Bear canisters mandatory, campfires banned outright at this height.
bivy.capacity: A primitive designated area rather than a developed camp; a handful of tent spots, no toilet you should count on

bivy.name: Sol Duc Hot Springs Resort campground
bivy.notes: The drive-in staging base for every objective in this zone except Mount Angeles, a couple of miles short of the end of the Sol Duc Hot Springs Road where the trailhead for the High Divide and Appleton Pass sits. Climbers use it the night before, because the walk to Heart Lake or Appleton Pass is long enough that leaving Port Angeles in the morning wastes the day. It opens with the season, roughly late March into late October, and it fills solidly on summer weekends. It is a staging base and nothing more — from here you still have the entire approach ahead of you, and every camp above it is permit-controlled.
bivy.water: Potable water and flush toilets in the comfort stations through the operating season
bivy.permit: No wilderness permit — this is a frontcountry campground with a nightly fee, taken on the federal recreation booking site or through the resort. Park entrance fee applies. Fires are allowed in the provided rings here, unlike anywhere you are going above it.
bivy.capacity: Around 82 tent sites plus a smaller RV loop; most tent sites are reservable and a handful are held back first-come

bivy.name: Boston Charlie's Camp
bivy.notes: This is the first camp on the far side of the Catwalk and the recognised start of the Bailey Range proper. It matters because it puts you directly at the foot of Mount Carrie's southwest ridge, where the route gains around 2,000 ft in under a mile on a semi-cairned bootpack, so a party camped here can be on the summit early and off the loose ground before the afternoon. Getting to it means crossing the exposed class 3 ridge between Cat Peak and Carrie with a full pack, which is the crux of the approach for most people and not somewhere to be in wet weather. The water is the honest drawback and the reason some parties push straight through to the basins beyond.
bivy.water: Poor and the standing complaint about the place — a shallow sinkhole pond that is often silty and stagnant, and nothing else nearby. Filter and treat, and consider carrying from Heart Lake or Cat Basin
bivy.permit: Covered by an Olympic wilderness cross-country permit, which for the Bailey Range is arranged directly with the park's wilderness information office rather than booked as a named campsite online. Bear canisters mandatory. No fires. Camp on durable surfaces — snow, rock or gravel — and pack out everything.
bivy.capacity: Informal cross-country bivy sites for a couple of small parties; no facilities of any kind

earlier_research.correct_value: Camping within Snowgrass Flat is prohibited; the approach must not recommend camping in the flat. The itinerary's higher camp (~7,100-7,200 ft, above the flat) is unaffected.
earlier_research.evidence: The Gifford Pinchot wilderness regulations prohibit camping within Snowgrass Flat and Shoe Lake Basin; a trail guide repeats that camping at Snowgrass Flat is prohibited and places the lower portion of the flat at the Lily Basin junction (4.1 mi). A trip report camped near 7,200 ft above the basin, consistent with the itinerary. Approach, approach variant and the Lily Basin junction waypoint note no longer present the flat as a camp. One trip report gives 14.2 mi round trip for the two-summit trip (matching totalNote) and a camp near 7,200 ft, but no source gives the trailhead-to-camp or camp-to-trailhead distance, so the 7 mi in vs 6.5 mi out vs summit-at-7-mi cannot be settled.

The schedule (5:30 AM to ~4:30-5 PM) implies ~11 h against 8 h in the day and timing. One trip report took 7.3 h for the Old Snowy/Ives loop from camp alone, which supports a longer day than 8 h with the hike-out, but no two sources state the day length, and changing it would cascade into timing.totalHrs.

One trip report gives ~2,400 ft for the Old Snowy/Ives loop from a lower camp; the stored 900 ft looks too low, but the itinerary total (2,500+900) equals gain_ft 3,400 and no source states this route's car-to-car gain for the two-summit plan, so per the rules no day figure is changed.

row.overview: Ives Peak (7,920+ ft) is the fourth-highest summit in the Goat Rocks Wilderness, sitting on the main crest between Old Snowy Mountain (7,880+ ft) to the north and Gilbert Peak (Mt. Curtis Gilbert), 8,184 ft, the range high point to the south. The peak straddles the Lewis/Yakima county line and is an eroded remnant of the Goat Rocks volcanic complex, an extinct stratovolcano active from roughly 3.2 million to 500,000 years ago; glaciation and hydrothermal alteration have since stripped away most of its outer flanks, exposing resistant volcanic dikes and spines. A small remnant glacier, the McCall Glacier, clings to Ives' northeast slope and feeds the Tieton River, while the west-facing slopes drain to the Cispus River. There is no maintained trail to the summit and nothing technical is required, but Ives sees only a fraction of the traffic of neighboring Old Snowy Mountain because of the off-trail travel and routefinding involved.
row.beta: The easiest way up Ives Peak is a scramble. The standard approach follows the Pacific Crest Trail / Goat Rocks crest, which runs close to the peak's western slopes, then leaves the crest at the col northwest of the peak and follows the northwest ridge and a short south-face scramble to the summit; this is unroped class 2-3 talus/scree, not a technical rock or ice route. A 2026 ski-mountaineering trip report (climberkyle.com) that circled the peak describes the ridge north of the summit as rocky and wind-scoured, with a short loose ('choss') section near the col, and notes lingering snow on the peak's flanks into early summer.
row.turnaround: As with any exposed alpine ridge scramble, set a turnaround time that gets you off the crest and below treeline before typical afternoon thunderstorm build-up, and before deteriorating visibility on featureless talus terrain.
row.face: Northwest ridge and upper south face of Ives Peak, reached from the Old Snowy-Ives col on the Goat Rocks crest

row.pro_needs: None — the standard route has no fixed protection or belays; consider an ice axe if snow still lingers on the crest or the peak's north/east-facing terrain early in the season.
row.best_season: Late July through September for reliable snow-free travel; snowfields on the approach and the glacier moat near the Old Snowy-Ives col can persist into July in heavy-snow years, and the range averages roughly 25-40 ft of snow most winters.
row.approach: Start at the Snowgrass Trailhead (aka "Berry Patch," elev. ~4,600 ft), reached via FR-21 (Johnson Creek Road) off US-12 about 3 miles west of Packwood. From the trailhead, follow the Snowgrass Trail #96 south then east through dense forest; the trail drops slightly (~75 ft) to cross Goat Creek on a footbridge/plank crossing around the 2-mile mark (only real water crossing on the approach, and a reliable water source — top off here or at the creeks in upper Snowgrass Flat). Continue climbing through subalpine forest and meadow to Lower Snowgrass Flat, then Upper Snowgrass Flat at roughly 6,400 ft (about 4 miles / ~1,800 ft gain from the trailhead) — a broad, popular wildflower meadow, closed to camping, with multiple small creeks (last dependable water before the ridge). From Upper Snowgrass Flat, continue about 0.3–0.5 mile further to the junction with the Pacific Crest Trail. Follow the PCT north to about 6,700 ft, then leave it and head off-trail to the northeast, ascending talus and scree with no defined tread (occasional cairns) toward the low col on the ridge crest between Old Snowy Mountain and Ives Peak — expect loose, unconsolidated talus that shifts underfoot; test holds and footing carefully. From the col, follow the ridge crest or a line just south of it (Class 2) over a rounded intermediate high point toward Ives' northwest ridge. At the base of the true summit block, a boot path threads up scree toward a notch between two rock outcrops; above the notch is a short cliff band — downclimb slightly and traverse a narrow, exposed ledge (Class 2) to gain the upper south face, then scramble roughly 40 ft to climber's right on loose blocky rock and up easy terrain to the 7,920-ft summit. Snowfields commonly linger on the approach slopes and in the col well into July (this basin can hold 25–40 ft of winter snowpack), so an ice axe is worth carrying for early/mid-season attempts on the traverse.
row.descent_text: Descend by reversing the ascent line: downclimb the loose Class 3 upper south face and the exposed ledge/cliff-band notch back to the northwest ridge, then follow the ridge crest back toward the Old Snowy–Ives col. From the col, most parties either (a) drop directly southwest through the scree/talus basin to regain the PCT — faster but the loosest, choss-iest line, or (b) traverse back over to Old Snowy Mountain and descend its established south-ridge boot path to the PCT near the Packwood Glacier bench, which several trip reports recommend specifically to avoid the worst loose rock directly below Ives' summit block. Either way, once back on the PCT, retrace it south to the Snowgrass Trail #96 junction and follow Snowgrass Trail #96 back down through Upper/Lower Snowgrass Flat and the Goat Creek crossing to the trailhead. This is entirely a scramble walk-off/downclimb — no fixed anchors, bolts, or rope work are involved or needed on this route. Primary descent hazards are the same loose talus/scree encountered on the ascent (higher consequence going downhill) and lingering snow/ice in the col and on the ridge crest into early-mid summer; a short glissade or scree-ski of the basin below the col is a common (optional) shortcut for the descent when snow-free.
row.bail: Retreat is straightforward along the same ridge/crest used for the ascent back toward Old Snowy Mountain and the maintained trail system below; there are no fixed rappel anchors on this route since it is unroped scramble terrain.

itinerary.cal: Free self-issue wilderness permits at the trailhead; the upper Snowgrass basin is typically not fully snow-free until mid-to-late July, and Snowgrass Flat proper is closed to camping so camp at established sites in the upper basin or off-trail on durable ground.

Afternoon is free to scout the next day's route to Elk Pass and enjoy the meadows and wildflowers.

approach_variants.name: Snowgrass Trail, the PCT junction and the Old Snowy to Ives col
approach_variants.notes: Start at the Snowgrass trailhead, also called Berry Patch, at about 4,600 ft, reached by forest road off the highway west of Packwood. Follow Snowgrass Trail #96 south then east through dense forest; it drops slightly to cross Goat Creek on a plank crossing around the 2-mile mark, which is the only real water crossing and a reliable source. Climb through subalpine forest and meadow to Lower and then Upper Snowgrass Flat at roughly 6,400 ft, about 4 miles in — a broad wildflower meadow, closed to camping, with small creeks, the last dependable water before the ridge. Continue a further 0.3 to 0.5 mile to the PCT junction, follow the PCT north to about 6,700 ft, then leave it and head off-trail northeast, ascending talus and scree with no defined tread and only occasional cairns, toward the low col on the crest between Old Snowy Mountain and Ives Peak. The talus is unconsolidated and shifts underfoot. Snowfields linger on the approach slopes and in the col well into July — this basin can hold 25 to 40 ft of winter snowpack — so an axe is worth carrying for early and mid-season attempts.

approach_variants.baseFinding:
THE COL BETWEEN OLD SNOWY AND IVES IS THE ARRIVAL, AND YOU GET TO IT BY LEAVING A TRAIL, NOT BY FOLLOWING ONE.

Leave the PCT north of the Snowgrass Trail junction, at roughly 6,700 ft, and go off-trail NORTHEAST up talus. There is no tread. Occasional cairns are the only marks. If you are still on maintained trail you have not started the route.

YOU KNOW YOU ARE AT THE COL BECAUSE YOU ARE BETWEEN TWO PEAKS at about 7,250 ft — Old Snowy behind you, Ives ahead. A high point on one side only is not the col.

THE BUMP IS THE TRAP AND IT IS COUNTABLE: from the col the ridge crosses a ROUNDED INTERMEDIATE HIGH POINT before you reach the true summit block. THAT BUMP IS NOT THE SUMMIT. If you have not passed one rounded bump, you have not reached the summit block, whatever the ground in front of you looks like.

THE BASE OF THE SCRAMBLE IS A NOTCH BETWEEN TWO ROCK OUTCROPS, reached by a boot path up scree. And here is the test that settles it beyond doubt, because it is the opposite of what you expect at a summit block: ABOVE THE NOTCH IS A SHORT CLIFF BAND, AND THE ROUTE GOES DOWN FIRST. You downclimb slightly and traverse a narrow, exposed ledge to gain the upper south face, then scramble about 40 ft to climber's right on loose blocky rock to easy ground and the summit.

SO: IF THE LINE IN FRONT OF YOU ONLY GOES UP, YOU ARE AT THE WRONG NOTCH. Having to lose a little height at the notch is the confirmation.

DESCENT FINDING WORTH MAKING BEFORE YOU START: dropping straight southwest off the col into the basin is faster and is the loosest ground on the mountain. Traversing back over Old Snowy and down its established south-ridge path avoids the worst of it.

climbing_route.label: Ridge crest from the col
climbing_route.notes: From the low col on the crest between Old Snowy Mountain and Ives Peak, follow the ridge crest or a line just south of it over a rounded intermediate high point toward Ives' northwest ridge. Snowfields commonly linger in the col well into July, so an ice axe is worth carrying for early/mid-season attempts on the traverse.

climbing_route.label: Notch and exposed ledge traverse
climbing_route.notes: At the base of the true summit block a boot path threads up scree toward a notch between two rock outcrops; above the notch is a short cliff band — downclimb slightly and traverse a narrow, exposed ledge to gain the upper south face.

climbing_route.label: Upper south face to summit
climbing_route.notes: Scramble roughly 40 ft to climber's right on loose blocky rock, then up easy terrain to the 7,920-ft summit.

bivy.name: Snowgrass Flat area backcountry camps
bivy.notes: The standard base for Old Snowy and Ives Peak, and for the West Route on Gilbert. The name misleads: the flat proper is a closed meadow and the legal camping is in the timber and on the benches a little below it, around 6,000 to 6,300 feet, roughly three to four miles from the road. From here Old Snowy is a walk-up on a spur off the crest, Ives is a scree-and-ridge scramble off the col between the two, and Gilbert is a long committing day traversing goat ledges across Cispus Basin at 7,400 to 7,600 feet before the southwest slope. This is the most heavily used corner of the wilderness and the parking fills on weekdays, so arriving Friday evening for a Saturday climb is a poor plan. The meadows hold snow into July in a normal year, which is pleasant for the scrambles and awkward for finding a dry pitch.
bivy.water: Goat Creek and its tributaries run through the basin and are reliable well into the season; treat everything
bivy.permit: Goat Rocks Wilderness permit, free and self-issued from the box at the trailhead — no reservation and no fee. A Northwest Forest Pass or Interagency pass is required to park at Berry Patch or the Snowgrass trailhead. CAMPING WITHIN SNOWGRASS FLAT ITSELF IS PROHIBITED, along with camping within 100 feet of the Pacific Crest Trail and within 100 feet of any lake. Camp only in pre-existing sites.
bivy.capacity: Numerous established sites in the timber and benches below and around the meadow; no quota and no numbered pads, so capacity is whatever the pre-existing sites hold, and on summer weekends that is fully subscribed

bivy.name: Chambers Lake Campground
bivy.notes: The obvious drive-in base for the Goat Rocks crest, under a mile from both the Berry Patch and Snowgrass trailheads, so you can sleep at the car and be walking at first light without the four-mile carry to Snowgrass. That makes it the right choice for a car-to-car attempt on Old Snowy, and a sensible staging night before shouldering a pack for Ives or Gilbert. It is heavily timbered and low, so there is no view and no acclimatisation value, and the approach roads are long gravel with washboard — allow more driving time than the mileage suggests. Snow closes the access road well into spring, which is the practical limit on early-season attempts from this side.

row.overview: A non-technical summit on the Okanogan Range crest between Rainy Pass and Washington Pass, in Chelan County within the Okanogan-Wenatchee National Forest. Whistler is linked by a high ridge to Cutthroat Peak (8,050 ft), 0.8 mile north-northeast, and offers a broad, mostly-talus scramble popular as an early-season warm-up or a corn-snow ski descent in late spring. The standard route climbs the mountain's south ridge and southwest slope; a steeper alternative ascends a broad gully system visible from Rainy Pass.
row.beta: From a roadside turnout on SR-20 (or alternatively the Rainy Pass PCT trailhead), a boot path climbs through open forest and a meadow basin, then rises on a traversing line to intersect the level part of Whistler's south ridge at about 6,180 ft. From there the route follows the ridge and adjoining gullies — staying north of a loose gully band and using a visible ramp near the headwall — to the 7,790 ft summit; an alternative continues the ridge to about 6,800 ft before cutting left across gullies onto gentler terrain on the southwest slope for the final push. It is class 3 scrambling throughout, with class 4 moves possible depending on line choice.
row.turnaround: In spring/early summer when the gullies still hold snow, turn around by late morning to avoid wet-slab avalanche release as the sun softens the snowpack; on the dry-season south-ridge route, the main time pressure is afternoon thunderstorm buildup over the crest.
row.permit: No climbing or wilderness permit required; Northwest Forest Pass (or day fee) to park at developed trailheads.
row.descent: Reverse the ascent route down the south ridge / southwest slope.
obj_haz: Cornices along the upper ridge and gully rims in winter/spring
Wet, heavy maritime snow prone to wet-slab avalanches

row.detailed_rack: No roped protection is used on the standard scramble route; parties typically carry trekking poles for the meadow/traverse sections, a helmet for the loose ridge and gully terrain, and an ice axe (with willingness to turn back if conditions warrant crampons) when snow lingers in the gullies in early season.

Layers for an exposed, wind-prone ridge
pro_tips: The Rainy Pass PCT-lot gully approach doubles as a well-regarded spring corn-snow ski descent — go early enough to catch the snow softening but before it turns to mush
On the south-ridge route, cutting left across gullies at ~6,800 ft onto the southwest slope avoids the harder gully scrambling higher on the ridge crest
watch_out: Trailhead access disappears entirely once SR 20's winter gates close (roughly late Nov–late Apr/mid-May) — check WSDOT pass status first

Early-season (May-June) ascents will find the gullies holding consolidated snow — carry an ice axe and know how to self-arrest
The west-gully descent funnels toward a seasonal waterfall — exit right into the glades to avoid it
row.pro_needs: None — this is an unroped Class 3 scramble with no fixed protection or technical rack; a rope and basic protection could be carried by conservative parties for the class 4 variations, but are not standard.
row.approach: Two trailheads serve the Southeast Slopes / South Ridge scramble, both off SR-20 between Rainy Pass and Washington Pass. Option A (PCT approach, most commonly used): park at the marked Pacific Crest Trail North trailhead lot on the north side of Rainy Pass (~4,850 ft, next to the Road 600 turnoff). From the lot, leave the PCT almost immediately and strike out cross-country/climber's-path east into open forest, gaining steeply through timber and over downed logs — there is no maintained tread once you leave the PCT. Continue up through the trees (expect lingering snow patches into early summer) to about 6,100 ft, where the forest opens into a meadow basin below the west ridge/gully complex. From the basin, trend south/southeast on a rising traverse to gain the col/basin between Whistler and the southwest peak of Cutthroat, then work up the broad west ridge or the shallow gully just north of it to the summit shoulder; the final short section involves a rock gully with a visible ramp along the headwall over downsloping slabs and loose gravel — a helmet is recommended here for rockfall from parties above. Round trip via this line runs roughly 3.7 miles with about 3,000 ft of gain (trailhead 4,850 ft to summit 7,790 ft). Option B (highway turnout approach, reaches the true south ridge): from the unmarked pullout on SR-20 about 3.1 miles east of Rainy Pass (0.7 mile before the Blue Lake trailhead, ~5,000 ft), walk back down/along the road shoulder to a boot path that starts at the west edge of a stand of trees. Follow the boot path up through a meadow, then rising-traverse to intersect the level portion of Whistler's south ridge at about 6,180 ft. From there, scramble up the ridge and connecting gullies to the summit; alternatively leave the ridge around 6,800 ft, cross a couple of gullies left (west) onto gentler southwest-facing slopes, and finish to the summit that way. This line is also about 4 miles round trip with ~3,000 ft gain. Both approaches are trail-less above the first stretch of forest — expect route-finding, loose talus/scree in the gullies, and class 2-3 terrain with occasional class 3-4 moves and real exposure near the ridge crest and summit gully; no reliable water source above the lower forest, so carry what you need from the car. No creek fords or avalanche paths of note on the standard summer line, but early-season snow lingers in the forest and basin and can make the gully sections firm or icy.
row.descent_text: There is no rappelling on the standard Southeast Slopes/South Ridge route — it's a walk-off/downclimb, reversing whichever line was used on the way up. From the summit, downclimb the summit gully (loose gravel and downsloping slabs — take care with rockfall for anyone below) back to the shoulder, then descend either the west ridge/gully back into the meadow basin and forest (Option A) or drop onto the south ridge and retrace the rising traverse back to the meadow and boot path to the highway turnout (Option B). Loose rock and talus in the gullies is the main descent hazard — down-climb facing in on the steeper class 3 sections and stay alert for parties below. Some ski mountaineers descend a separate snow-filled west gully (~35°, over 1,000 ft of sustained fall-line terrain funneling to a waterfall lower down, requiring an exit right into the glades to avoid the falls) as a spring ski descent, but that is a snow-season variant, not part of the standard summer scramble descent, and should not be used as a hiking descent once snow is out. rappels: 0.
row.bail: Retreat is straightforward by reversing the scramble at any point; no committing technical sections.

road.driveNote: Drive SR 20 over Rainy Pass; the two trailhead options (Rainy Pass PCT lot, or the unmarked pullout 3.1 mi east of the pass) are both directly off the highway with no additional dirt-road driving.
road.seasonalGate: Gated closed for winter — gates at Diablo (west) and Early Winters near Mazama (east). Typically closes late November and reopens late April to mid-May depending on snowpack; check WSDOT's pass report before planning a trip.

climate.fall: Cools quickly with possible early-season snow at elevation; SR-20 access can end abruptly with the season's first significant highway closure.
climate.spring: Snowpack still substantial into May/June on north- and gully-facing terrain; the west-facing gully is a documented corn-snow ski descent in late May.
climate.summer: Generally dry with occasional afternoon thunderstorms typical of the eastern Cascades crest; the standard scramble window.
climate.winter: SR-20 gated/closed through the Washington Pass-Rainy Pass corridor; the peak is inaccessible by the standard trailhead.
climate.typical: Marine west coast climate with a strong maritime influence even on this east-slope Cascades peak; winter and spring snow tends to be wet and heavy, producing high avalanche danger on the gullied approaches. Summers are typically dry with mostly clear skies, though afternoon thunderstorms can build over the Cascade crest.

bySeason.fall: Good scrambling into September/early October; watch for early-season snow and shortening daylight.
bySeason.spring: Deep, often unstable wet snow fills the gullies (used for ski descents); avalanche and cornice hazard is significant — check NWAC before going.
bySeason.summer: Typical dry-scramble season once snow clears the upper slopes, usually by mid-to-late July; talus and scree underfoot.

emergency.notes: Cell coverage is unreliable to absent in the Rainy Pass/Washington Pass corridor; the nearest reliable help is the highway itself — flag down traffic or drive to Mazama/Winthrop. This stretch of SR 20 is remote and, once winter gates close, entirely inaccessible.

approach_variants.name: Rainy Pass PCT lot, then cross-country east into the meadow basin and the col toward Cutthroat's southwest peak
approach_variants.notes:
Park at the marked Pacific Crest Trail North trailhead lot on the north side of Rainy Pass at about 4,850 ft, next to the Road 600 turnoff. LEAVE THE PCT ALMOST IMMEDIATELY and strike out cross-country east into open forest, gaining steeply through timber and over downed logs. There is no maintained tread once you leave the PCT.

This is WHISTLER MOUNTAIN ABOVE RAINY PASS in Chelan County, not the Whistler Canyon trailhead area near Oroville, which is about 100 miles away and unrelated.

Round trip runs roughly 3.7 miles with about 3,000 ft of gain.
hazards: No maintained tread above the PCT; route-finding the whole way
Downed logs in the lower forest
Loose talus and scree in the gullies, with class 3-4 moves and real exposure near the ridge crest
Downsloping slabs and loose gravel in the summit gully
No reliable water above the lower forest
Early-season snow lingering in the forest and basin, firming the gullies
approach_variants.baseFinding:
CLIMB UNTIL THE FOREST OPENS. At about 6,100 ft the timber gives way to A MEADOW BASIN BELOW THE WEST RIDGE AND GULLY COMPLEX, and that transition is the first reliable confirmation on a trail-less approach. Trees stopping is something you notice in any visibility.

FROM THE BASIN, TREND SOUTH AND SOUTHEAST ON A RISING TRAVERSE TO GAIN THE COL AND BASIN BETWEEN WHISTLER AND THE SOUTHWEST PEAK OF CUTTHROAT. THAT COL IS THE AIMING POINT, and it is named by the two peaks either side of it.

Then work up the BROAD WEST RIDGE, or the SHALLOW GULLY JUST NORTH OF IT, to the summit shoulder.

THE LAST SECTION IS THE ONE THAT CONFIRMS YOU ARE ON THE SUMMIT LINE RATHER THAN A NEIGHBOURING GULLY: A ROCK GULLY WITH A VISIBLE RAMP ALONG THE HEADWALL, OVER DOWNSLOPING SLABS AND LOOSE GRAVEL. A ramp cutting the headwall is the way through; helmet on here for rockfall from parties above.

approach_variants.name: The unmarked SR-20 turnout, then a boot path onto the true south ridge at 6,180 ft
approach_variants.notes:
The second option, and the one that reaches the true south ridge. From the unmarked pullout on SR-20 about 3.1 miles east of Rainy Pass, 0.7 mile BEFORE the Blue Lake trailhead, at about 5,000 ft, walk back down and along the road shoulder to a boot path that starts at the WEST EDGE OF A STAND OF TREES.

About 4 miles round trip with roughly 3,000 ft of gain, the same as the PCT option.
hazards: An unmarked trailhead identified only by its distance from the Blue Lake trailhead
Trail-less above the first stretch of forest
Class 2-3 with occasional class 3-4 moves and real exposure near the ridge crest
Loose talus and scree in the connecting gullies
No reliable water on the route
approach_variants.baseFinding:
THE TRAILHEAD IS UNMARKED AND THE PATH START IS A TREE-LINE EDGE, SO THE FIND IS AT THE ROAD RATHER THAN ON THE MOUNTAIN. The pullout is 0.7 MILE BEFORE THE BLUE LAKE TRAILHEAD coming from Rainy Pass. IF YOU HAVE REACHED THE BLUE LAKE TRAILHEAD, YOU HAVE DRIVEN 0.7 MILE TOO FAR. From the pullout, walk the shoulder to where a STAND OF TREES begins, and the boot path leaves from its WEST EDGE.

FOLLOW THE BOOT PATH UP THROUGH A MEADOW, THEN RISING-TRAVERSE TO INTERSECT THE LEVEL PORTION OF WHISTLER'S SOUTH RIDGE AT ABOUT 6,180 FT. A LEVEL SECTION OF RIDGE IS THE ARRIVAL, and a level stretch on a ridge is something you can feel underfoot without seeing anything.

FROM THERE, SCRAMBLE UP THE RIDGE AND CONNECTING GULLIES TO THE SUMMIT. THE ALTERNATIVE, WHICH IS ALSO CORRECT: leave the ridge around 6,800 ft, cross a couple of gullies LEFT, west, onto gentler southwest-facing slopes, and finish that way.

SO THE DECISION AT 6,800 FT IS A REAL FORK AND BOTH BRANCHES WORK: stay on the crest for more exposure and directness, or cross two gullies west for easier ground.

THE NEGATIVE TEST AGAINST THE OTHER APPROACH, WHICH MATTERS BECAUSE BOTH START WITHIN THREE MILES OF EACH OTHER ON THE SAME HIGHWAY: the PCT option leaves from the marked PCT North lot at Rainy Pass and gains a MEADOW BASIN at 6,100 ft below the WEST ridge. This one leaves from an unmarked turnout and gains the SOUTH ridge at 6,180 ft. Marked lot and west ridge, or unmarked turnout and south ridge.

climbing_route.notes: From the meadow basin at about 6,100 ft trend south/southeast on a rising traverse to gain the col/basin between Whistler and the southwest peak of Cutthroat, then work up the broad west ridge or the shallow gully just north of it to the summit shoulder. Trail-less with route-finding and loose talus/scree in the gullies, and real exposure near the ridge crest; early-season snow can make the gully sections firm or icy.

climbing_route.notes: Intersect the level portion of Whistler's south ridge at about 6,180 ft, then scramble up the ridge and connecting gullies to the summit; loose talus/scree in the gullies and real exposure near the ridge crest and summit gully.

climbing_route.notes: Alternatively leave the ridge around 6,800 ft, cross a couple of gullies left (west) onto gentler southwest-facing slopes, and finish to the summit that way.

bivy.name: Rainy Pass PCT north trailhead
bivy.notes: Everything starts from this lot. It is also the start of Whistler Mountain, which is unlike the rest: head east from the parking area into the second gully and follow it to the summit, about four miles round trip and three thousand feet of gain, and no camp helps in the slightest. There is a toilet and no water. Parties routinely sleep in the car here before a long PCT day. As with everything on this stretch of SR 20, access is governed by the winter closure — the highway shuts in late November or early December and normally reopens between mid April and early May, though a bad winter can push it very much later, so confirm before driving. Note also that this specific trailhead has been closed at times for roadwork in recent seasons, which strands the entire zone when it happens.
bivy.water: None at the lot, and this matters more here than it looks. The crest north of the pass is dry, so what you carry out of the car is what you have until well down the far side.
bivy.permit: Northwest Forest Pass or Interagency pass to park. No camping permit, no quota and nothing to reserve anywhere in this zone — this is national forest, and the park permit system that governs the country west of here does not apply.
bivy.capacity: A large paved lot on the north-east side of the highway at the pass, shared between climbers, larch-season day hikers and long-distance walkers. It fills early on weekends from late summer onward and there is no overflow.

approach_logistics.trailhead: SR-20 pullout near milepost 165-166 (Silver Star / Wine Spires)

approach_variants.name: SR-20 pullout, Burgundy Creek climbers' trail, the Bench, Burgundy Col
approach_variants.notes:
Park at the broad pullout and overlook on SR-20 near milepost 165-166, about four miles east of Washington Pass, where a sign points toward Silver Star Mountain.

Drop down the embankment roughly 150 to 200 ft to Early Winters Creek and cross on a log. Logjams shift year to year, so scout up and down for the best crossing and be prepared to ford in high water or early season when the creek runs cold and fast with snowmelt. Treat this crossing as your LAST RELIABLE WATER until camp.

On the far bank pick up the unofficial but well-defined climbers' trail that climbs the timbered rib on the WEST (left) side of the Burgundy Creek drainage. From there it climbs relentlessly and steeply through forest and brush for roughly 2,500-3,000 ft with almost no switchbacks and only fleeting water access early on. The tread erodes and is easy to lose in the timber.
hazards: Early Winters Creek crossing — log can be wet, mossy or washed out; ford in high water
Steep eroding brushy tread that is easy to lose in the timber
Loose microwave-sized blocks in the gully bed above the bench
Loose kitty-litter slabs on the final traverse into the col
No water between the creek and the bench
approach_variants.baseFinding:
The unmistakable break on this approach is THE BENCH, at roughly 6,400-6,700 ft: the grade suddenly eases onto an open larch-and-heather shelf with several established campsites and usually a seasonal trickle or snowmelt nearby. That is the standard overnight camp and the natural turnaround check for a day trip.

Above the bench there is a gully running obviously and directly to Burgundy Col. THAT GULLY IS THE WRONG ONE — it is loose and exposed. Instead stay LEFT and follow the trail up the gully directly above camp. Within it, stay climber's LEFT of the gully proper: the bed holds loose microwave-sized blocks, while the left side is unpleasant kitty-litter-covered slab but far less dangerous. Near the head of the gully make an ascending traverse to the RIGHT, under the cliffs, over heather-covered slabs into the col at roughly 7,800 ft. This gully and traverse is where parties describe the real crux of route-finding, both up and down. The col — not the glacier — is where the route proper begins; from there trend toward the northeast side of the west summit.

bivy.name: Burgundy Creek bench camp — WEST side
bivy.notes: The flat, sheltered alternative to sleeping at the col, in trees before the timbered rib gives way to open scree. Reports consistently call it the more pleasant camp of the two, at the cost of extra vertical on summit morning. Elevation is quoted anywhere from about 6,400 to 6,500 ft depending on which flat spot a party used. Its value is almost entirely the spring: if that has failed, the bench loses most of its advantage over the col.
bivy.water: The most dependable water on this approach, but NOT from the obvious place. The creek shown on maps immediately east of the bench is frequently dry, while a spring roughly ten minutes north of camp keeps running well into September in most years. Confirm it before committing, and expect insects around it.
bivy.permit: None required. Okanogan-Wenatchee National Forest, non-wilderness, so no permit or reservation applies.
bivy.capacity: Several established tent spots on a wooded bench, with a large boulder and an old fire ring as the usual landmark; comfortably three or four tents

bivy.name: Burgundy Col high camp — WEST side, the Wine Spires
bivy.notes: The narrow saddle between Burgundy Spire and the ridge, and the standard high camp for the Wine Spires and for the Silver Star Glacier approached from the highway side. Published elevations disagree by a couple of hundred feet, with figures from roughly 7,720 to 7,950 in circulation, so treat any single number as approximate. It is exposed to wind from both sides and several parties have dropped back down the west slope to sleep after a rough night. Camping here removes about 1,500 ft of the scree from summit day, which is most of the argument for carrying overnight gear up it.
bivy.water: No spring or stream. Parties melt snow from the lingering patches on the glacier side of the col, which normally hold into late summer but can be rock-hard in the morning or gone entirely in a dry, late season. Many simply haul all their water up the scree, which is the single heaviest decision on this approach.
bivy.permit: None. Okanogan-Wenatchee National Forest, outside any designated wilderness — no quota, no reservation and no self-issue permit, unlike the North Cascades park zones a few miles west.
bivy.capacity: Two to four rock-ringed bivy platforms; roughly one is level enough for a two-person tent, so a large party should expect to sleep scattered or send some members back down

bivy.name: Lone Fir Campground, SR 20
bivy.notes: A roadside vehicle campground rather than a site on any approach — it is for sleeping the night before, not for the climb. It opens around May and closes with the first serious snow, tracking the same window as everything else here. The whole area is gated by the SR 20 winter closure, which shuts in late November or early December and reopens in spring, with the date driven by avalanche work and storm damage rather than the calendar. In closed months the pullout is inside the gated section and the approach becomes a long ski or snowmobile trip.
bivy.water: No drinking water at the campground. Early Winters Creek runs alongside and needs filtering; Klipchuck and Early Winters campgrounds, farther east, have drinking water in season.
bivy.permit: Per-night campground fee; no wilderness permit involved. The unmarked Silver Star Creek pullout that starts the west approach is not itself a signed fee site — check current signage rather than assuming either way.
bivy.capacity: 27 developed first-come, first-served sites for tents and small vehicles

bivy.name: Upper scree benches below Burgundy Col — WEST side
bivy.notes: Not an established campsite so much as a fallback for a party that has run out of daylight or water partway up the talus. The main reason to know about them is that the water situation on this hillside is patchy rather than uniform, so a dry creek at the wooded bench does not necessarily mean a dry mountainside above it. Anyone counting on this should carry a stove and be prepared to find nothing.
bivy.water: Genuinely unreliable and conditions-dependent. At least one party found a trickle running here in a season when the bench camp creek below was dry, which makes it worth checking on the way up, but nothing about it is dependable enough to plan a camp around.
bivy.permit: None. Non-wilderness National Forest land; no permit, quota or registration.
bivy.capacity: Improvised, one or two small parties at most; flat ground has to be found or built rather than chosen

row.name: Silver Star Glacier
row.fa: Fred Beckey, Joe Heib, Herb Staley and Don Wilde, May 1952
gear: Harness plus a few slings/carabiners for the summit scramble
Glacier travel rope and pickets (crevasses possible after mid-summer)

row.overview: The easiest and most popular route to the true (east, 8,876 ft) summit of Silver Star Mountain, climbing one of the easternmost glaciers in the Cascade Range. From Burgundy Col the route drops onto the glacier's north side, traverses beneath Burgundy Spire, and climbs roughly 1,500 ft of moderate snow/glacier to the saddle between Silver Star's two summits, finishing with a 3rd-to-low-5th-class rock scramble to the summit block. First climbed by Lage Wernstedt in 1926, though from the south side rather than this now-standard north-glacier line.
row.beta: Classic alpine glacier climb combining sustained elevation gain, moderate glacier navigation, and exciting exposed scrambling. Two summit options (east and west separated by 300-ft col). The north-side glacier gains approximately 1,500 feet with increasing steepness toward summit. Upper glacier can have crevasses requiring cautious navigation, especially late season. Final 300-500 feet involves scrambling rated 3rd to low 5th class to true summit; many climbers stop at slightly lower, easier point.
row.turnaround: Aim to be off the glacier and through the loose Burgundy Col gully before early-mid afternoon to avoid thunderstorms and softened, sun-rotten snow.
row.permit: No climbing or wilderness permit required; no parking pass is needed at the SR-20 pullout.
row.comms: No cell service at Burgundy Col or on glacier. Highway 20 is accessible mid-April to December, weather permitting; typically closed Dec-Mar. Emergency: Okanogan County Sheriff Dispatch (non-emergency 509-422-7232, 911 for life-threatening emergencies). Okanogan County Sheriff at 509-422-7200.
row.descent: Reverse the ascent: back down the glacier, up and over Burgundy Col, then down the climber's trail.

row.detailed_rack: Standard glacier-mountaineering kit: ice axe, crampons, a rope with crevasse-rescue gear, and a helmet; a light rock rack is optional for the final class 3-4 scrambling to the east summit.
pro_tips: Many parties camp on the larch bench (~6,400 ft) rather than the more exposed, windier Burgundy Col
Start early enough to cross the glacier and descend the sandy Burgundy Col gully before afternoon storms build
No parking pass is needed at the SR-20 pullout; the developed trailheads nearby, such as Blue Lake and Cutthroat, do require a Northwest Forest Pass
row.pro_needs: Primarily snow and glacier protection; minimal rock pro for the short scramble finish.
row.best_season: Mid-July through September for the most consolidated glacier conditions.
row.approach: Park at the broad pullout/overlook on SR-20 near milepost 165–166 (about 4 miles east of Washington Pass), where a sign points toward Silver Star Mountain. From the pullout, drop down the embankment roughly 150–200 ft to Early Winters Creek and cross on a log (logjams shift year to year — scout up- and downstream for the best crossing, and be ready to ford in high water/early season, when the creek runs cold and fast with snowmelt). On the far bank, pick up the unofficial but well-defined climber's trail that climbs the timbered rib on the west (left) side of the Burgundy Creek drainage. From here the trail climbs relentlessly and steeply through forest and brush for roughly 2,500–3,000 ft with almost no switchbacks and only fleeting creek-side water access early on — treat the crossing at Early Winters Creek as your last reliable water until camp. At around 6,000–6,400 ft the grade eases at 'the Bench,' an open larch-and-heather shelf with several established campsites and usually a seasonal trickle or snowmelt nearby; this is the standard overnight camp for a two-day trip and a natural break point/turnaround check for day-trippers. Above the bench, continue up open subalpine terrain toward Burgundy Col. Do not take the obvious direct gully to the col — it is loose and exposed; instead stay left, follow the trail up the gully directly above camp, and near its head make an ascending traverse right under the cliffs on heather-covered slabs into the col itself (roughly 7,800 ft). Total gain from the highway to the col is on the order of 3,500–4,400 ft depending on exact trailhead/camp used. Hazards on the approach: the Early Winters Creek crossing (cold, log can be wet/mossy or washed out), steep eroding/brushy tread that's easy to lose in the timber, and loose rock ('kitty litter') on the final gully/traverse into the col.
row.descent_text: Descend by reversing the ascent route. From the summit, downclimb the short class 3–4 rock (the same easy, somewhat exposed ledge system used on the way up) back to the col between the east and west summits; several trip reports and topo photos document a natural/slung rappel anchor near the true summit that parties use to bypass the most exposed section of this downclimb — a single rappel with one 50 m rope (or a 60 m rope doubled) is enough to get below the crux and onto easier ground, though plenty of parties simply downclimb the whole way and skip it entirely, so treat this as an optional, not mandatory, rappel with a natural anchor (sling on a horn/block), not bolts. From the base of the summit scramble, work back down onto the Silver Star Glacier and re-descend it, wrapping below the rock slabs of Burgundy Spire; note that this traverse dips below the elevation of Burgundy Col, so you must reclimb a couple hundred feet of steep snow from the low point back up to the col — a sting in the tail that catches parties expecting a pure descent. From Burgundy Col, downclimb the steep snow and loose, unstable 'kitty litter' rock/gully back toward the bench; this section is notoriously slow and has taken parties 3+ hours in reported descents. From the bench, follow the climber's trail back down through the timber to Early Winters Creek, re-cross (log or ford), and climb the short embankment back up to the SR-20 pullout. A less common alternative is to descend the east side via the Silver Star Creek basin instead of reversing to Burgundy Col (avoiding the reclimb to the col), but this exits at a different highway pullout and requires a car shuttle or road walk back, so most parties simply reverse the ascent.
row.bail: Retreat is straightforward by reversing the glacier, conditions permitting.

Aero Methow Rescue Service (based in Twisp, with stations in Winthrop and Mazama) provides the closest EMS/ambulance response and coordinates with Okanogan County Search and Rescue on backcountry evacuations; Washington Pass is roughly 30-40 minutes from Winthrop when the highway is open.
emergency.rangerStation: Methow Valley Ranger District, 24 West Chewuch Rd, Winthrop, WA
emergency.nearestHospital: Three Rivers Hospital (Brewster) and Mid-Valley Hospital (Omak) are the nearest full hospitals, roughly 70-75 miles / 1.5+ hours from the trailhead via SR-20 and Hwy 97.
emergency.sheriffDispatch: Okanogan County Sheriff non-emergency dispatch: (509) 422-7232 (or 800-572-6604 within the 509 area code); dial 911 for active emergencies.

crowds.peakTraffic: Weekends mid-July through August, especially when paired with a Mountaineers-style overnight club trip
crowds.estimatePerSeason: Likely the busiest route on the peak (guide services and clubs both run it), but still a remote glaciated objective — rough estimate 20-40 parties over a season, well below trailhead-access scrambles closer to Seattle

fitnessSpec.hiking: Long, sustained approach and summit day — commonly done as an overnight but fit parties push it in a single very long day (10-14+ hrs car-to-car)
fitnessSpec.packWeight: Overnight glacier kit (rope, crevasse-rescue gear, camping gear) unless doing a fast single push, so moderate-to-heavy pack

partner_requirements.approachTime: Long approach via Burgundy Col to the glacier basin; most parties camp partway rather than day-tripping it
requiredSkills: Class 3-4 scrambling with exposure near the summit
partner_requirements.experienceLevel: Intermediate mountaineer comfortable with roped glacier travel and crevasse rescue; not a beginner objective despite the class 3-4 rating

seasonal_guidance.optimalWindow: Mid-July through September — glacier is most consolidated and crevasse bridges most predictable in this window

July.reason: Improves through the month as snowpack consolidates; early July can still carry lingering avalanche and soft-bridge crevasse risk

June.reason: Deep, unconsolidated snow and unstable/unbridged crevasses; early-season avalanche hazard on the north-facing glacier

August.reason: Most consolidated glacier conditions and lowest avalanche hazard of the season

October.reason: Early-season snowfall can return, shortening daylight and reintroducing avalanche concerns before the route re-freezes for winter

September.reason: Stable weather and open glacier, but crevasses are most exposed/visible late season, requiring careful route-finding around them

weather.typical: Washington Pass sits on the drier east side of the Cascade crest but still catches wet, heavy maritime storm systems; wet, heavy snow drives avalanche danger
weather.probability: Afternoon convective buildups are possible in mid-summer; approach and summit day are best done with an early alpine start to avoid deteriorating afternoon weather

seasonal_hazards.exposure: Moderate: crevasse-fall risk on the glacier, plus real but bounded exposure on the final class 3-4 rock to the east summit, which is loose

avalanche.zone: NWAC East Slopes North (Washington Pass area) — inferred from the Hwy 20/Washington Pass access corridor, not a peak-specific NWAC zone

seasonal_hazards.crevasses: Roped glacier travel required on the Silver Star Glacier; crevasse awareness is especially important later in the season as bridges thin and gaps open

gaps: No confirmed current crevasse/bergschrund status for the glacier - check recent trip reports before a late-season attempt

approach_variants.name: Burgundy Col and the glacier, in a day
approach_variants.notes:
Park at the pullout on SR-20 near milepost 166, about four miles east of Washington Pass. Drop the embankment — around 150 to 200 feet down loose ground — to Early Winters Creek and cross on a log; the logjam moves year to year, so scout, and be ready to ford in early-season high water.

On the far side pick up the well-defined climbers' path up the timbered rib on the west side of the Burgundy Creek drainage. It climbs steeply and almost without switchbacks. Treat the creek as your last reliable water.

Around 6,000 to 6,400 ft the grade eases at the bench, an open larch and heather shelf with established campsites. Above it, continue toward Burgundy Col — roughly 3,500 ft of gain from the highway to the col.

Do not take the obvious direct gully to the col: it is loose and exposed. Stay left, follow the trail up the gully directly above the camp area, and near its head make an ascending traverse right under the cliffs on heather-covered slabs into the col at about 7,770 ft.
hazards: Early Winters Creek crossing — log can be wet or washed out, ford is cold and fast in early season
steep eroding brushy tread in the timber, easy to lose
loose ball-bearing rock on the final gully and traverse into the col
crevasses on the upper glacier, more open late season
the return traverse drops BELOW the elevation of Burgundy Col, so the descent includes a couple of hundred feet of reclimbing steep snow back up to the notch — parties are caught out by this
descending the loose ground below the col has taken parties three hours or more
approach_variants.baseFinding:
The col is not the start of the climbing — the glacier is on the FAR side of it. From Burgundy Col, descend roughly 200 feet of steep snow down the east side onto the Silver Star Glacier; that descent is the moment the route begins, and parties rope up at the edge of the glacier below it. Head east, climb to the flat top of a spur ridge, then traverse east onto the main body of the glacier and ascend south to the saddle just west of the summit.

The finish is where people get it wrong. From that saddle the summit is a short scramble east, but only on one line: look for an easy RAMP about 40 feet below the summit. Take it and the summit is class 3 to 4. Miss it and you end up on a short pitch of low fifth class instead. In poor visibility, work generally left off the saddle and hunt for the ramp rather than committing to the first steep line you meet.

approach_variants.name: Camp at the bench, summit the second day
approach_variants.notes:
The same line from the milepost 166 pullout, broken at the open bench at roughly 6,000 to 6,400 ft where the climbers' path first eases. There are several established sites there, usually with a seasonal trickle or snowmelt nearby, and it is the standard overnight for this peak.

Camping here means you cross the glacier on firm morning snow and are back over the col before the afternoon softening, which matters given the reclimb to the col on the way out.
hazards: the direct gully to the col is the wrong line — loose and exposed
no water above the bench once the seasonal trickle dries
crevasses on the upper glacier
the reclimb back up to Burgundy Col at the end of the day
approach_variants.baseFinding: From the bench, follow the trail up the gully directly above camp — not the obvious direct gully toward the col, which is loose and exposed — and near its head traverse rightward under the cliffs on heather slabs into Burgundy Col. Then drop about 200 feet of steep snow off the east side of the col onto the Silver Star Glacier and rope up at the glacier's edge. The col has Burgundy Spire on one side and Paisano Pinnacle on the other, and a glacier behind it; if there is no glacier on the far side, it is not the col.

bivy.name: Burgundy Col high camp — WEST side, the Wine Spires
bivy.notes: The narrow saddle between Burgundy Spire and the ridge, and the standard high camp for the Wine Spires and for the Silver Star Glacier approached from the highway side. Published elevations disagree by a couple of hundred feet, with figures from roughly 7,720 to 7,950 in circulation, so treat any single number as approximate. It is exposed to wind from both sides and several parties have dropped back down the west slope to sleep after a rough night. Camping here removes about 1,500 ft of the scree from summit day, which is most of the argument for carrying overnight gear up it.
bivy.water: No spring or stream. Parties melt snow from the lingering patches on the glacier side of the col, which normally hold into late summer but can be rock-hard in the morning or gone entirely in a dry, late season. Many simply haul all their water up the scree, which is the single heaviest decision on this approach.
bivy.permit: None. Okanogan-Wenatchee National Forest, outside any designated wilderness — no quota, no reservation and no self-issue permit, unlike the North Cascades park zones a few miles west.
bivy.capacity: Two to four rock-ringed bivy platforms; roughly one is level enough for a two-person tent, so a large party should expect to sleep scattered or send some members back down

bivy.name: Burgundy Creek bench camp — WEST side
bivy.notes: The flat, sheltered alternative to sleeping at the col, in trees before the timbered rib gives way to open scree. Reports consistently call it the more pleasant camp of the two, at the cost of extra vertical on summit morning. Elevation is quoted anywhere from about 6,400 to 6,500 ft depending on which flat spot a party used. Its value is almost entirely the spring: if that has failed, the bench loses most of its advantage over the col.
bivy.water: The most dependable water on this approach, but NOT from the obvious place. The creek shown on maps immediately east of the bench is frequently dry, while a spring roughly ten minutes north of camp keeps running well into September in most years. Confirm it before committing, and expect insects around it.
bivy.permit: None required. Okanogan-Wenatchee National Forest, non-wilderness, so no permit or reservation applies.
bivy.capacity: Several established tent spots on a wooded bench, with a large boulder and an old fire ring as the usual landmark; comfortably three or four tents

bivy.name: Lone Fir Campground, SR 20
bivy.notes: A roadside vehicle campground rather than a site on any approach — it is for sleeping the night before, not for the climb. It opens around May and closes with the first serious snow, tracking the same window as everything else here. The whole area is gated by the SR 20 winter closure, which shuts in late November or early December and reopens in spring, with the date driven by avalanche work and storm damage rather than the calendar. In closed months the pullout is inside the gated section and the approach becomes a long ski or snowmobile trip.
bivy.water: No drinking water at the campground. Early Winters Creek runs alongside and needs filtering; Klipchuck and Early Winters campgrounds, farther east, have drinking water in season.
bivy.permit: Per-night campground fee; no wilderness permit involved. The unmarked Silver Star Creek pullout that starts the west approach is not itself a signed fee site — check current signage rather than assuming either way.
bivy.capacity: 27 developed first-come, first-served sites for tents and small vehicles

bivy.name: Upper scree benches below Burgundy Col — WEST side
bivy.notes: Not an established campsite so much as a fallback for a party that has run out of daylight or water partway up the talus. The main reason to know about them is that the water situation on this hillside is patchy rather than uniform, so a dry creek at the wooded bench does not necessarily mean a dry mountainside above it. Anyone counting on this should carry a stove and be prepared to find nothing.
bivy.water: Genuinely unreliable and conditions-dependent. At least one party found a trickle running here in a season when the bench camp creek below was dry, which makes it worth checking on the way up, but nothing about it is dependable enough to plan a camp around.
bivy.permit: None. Non-wilderness National Forest land; no permit, quota or registration.
bivy.capacity: Improvised, one or two small parties at most; flat ground has to be found or built rather than chosen
